idiom_name: BasicObject + method_missing proxy (or SimpleDelegator) in front of a privately held resource
implementation_notes: Ruby's idiom for the owning guard is a proxy object: subclass BasicObject - the alternate object hierarchy the docs recommend for proxies such as Delegator - define method_missing plus respond_to_missing?, and forward only after the policy agrees; the standard library's Delegator/SimpleDelegator does the forwarding for you and is the lighter option when the guard is a pure wrapper. Visibility is runtime-enforced (a visibility-violating call raises NoMethodError) but not adversarial: send/__send__, instance_variable_get and instance_eval reach private methods and ivars deliberately, so the guard's encapsulation is a design property rather than a boundary. For OS resources the same division holds as in the other dynamic languages: the permission bits on the file are enforced by the kernel, and in-process checks are only a design convention.
pitfalls: send/__send__, instance_variable_get and instance_eval defeat Ruby visibility by design, so the guard organizes ownership but cannot confine arbitrary code in the same process.

A BasicObject subclass loses Kernel/Object methods (inspect, raise, class, respond_to?): call them fully qualified (::Kernel.raise) and keep respond_to_missing? honest, or use SimpleDelegator which handles the protocol.

method_missing delegation makes the guard's surface the target's public surface - every method the store exposes becomes reachable unless the guard filters names; keep an allow-list for privileged resources.
Delegation must use public_send (or an explicit allow-list); plain send re-exposes the resource's private API to callers.
